summary:
XHEAL is a crew health and mission performance system designed for longduration space missions, particularly missions to Mars where communication with Earth can be delayed.

Instead of simply monitoring whether an astronaut's health measurements are within normal ranges, XHEAL examines how their physiological condition, psychological wellbeing, sleep, recovery and mission environment affect their ability to perform specific tasks.

It combines personal health baselines, sensor quality assessment, explainable causal reasoning and task specific capability assessments. It can recommend countermeasures, track crew decisions, verify observed changes and simulate alternative mission scenarios before decisions are made.

The system also integrates real astronaut research from NASA's Open Science Data Repository, alongside a clearly separated synthetic Mars mission simulation.

I built XHEAL around a simple question: what can an astronaut safely do under their current conditions, what is limiting them, and what can be changed?
details:
XHEAL — Earth-Independent Crew Health & Mission Performance Operating System

Human health monitoring becomes considerably more complicated during long-duration spaceflight. On a mission to Mars, communication delays can reach approximately 22 minutes one way. Crew members cannot depend on immediate ground intervention for every operational decision. At the same time, monitoring individual health measurements is not enough to determine whether an astronaut is capable of performing a particular mission task.

This is the problem I wanted to work on with XHEAL.

I built XHEAL as an integrated crew health and mission-performance system that connects physiological measurements, psychological wellbeing, environmental conditions and mission workload to actual operational capability.

How it works

XHEAL begins by collecting and organizing astronaut telemetry, health observations and mission-context data. Before interpreting measurements, it evaluates their quality and reliability. Missing, degraded or invalid sensor readings are explicitly identified rather than silently replaced.

The system then builds individual baselines and compares current measurements against each astronaut's own historical patterns. It uses robust statistical deviations and circadian-aware interpretation to identify meaningful changes without relying entirely on generic population thresholds.

These observations feed into a health-state inference system covering cardiovascular health, sleep, recovery, cognitive performance, environmental exposure, thermoregulation, operational conditions and psychological wellbeing.

However, identifying a health deviation is only part of the problem. XHEAL also needs to understand its operational consequences.

From health monitoring to mission capability

One of the main ideas behind XHEAL is that health state and mission capability are not the same thing.

An astronaut might be capable of performing routine habitat operations while requiring additional assessment before a physically demanding extravehicular activity.

XHEAL uses an explainable causal model to connect factors such as workload, sleep debt, recovery, cognitive performance and environmental stress to specific capability dimensions.

It evaluates different mission tasks independently and produces five possible states: GO, WATCH, CONDITIONAL, HOLD and UNKNOWN.

Every consequential assessment can be traced back through the measurements, sensor quality, personal baseline, inferred state and causal contributions that produced it.

Countermeasures and verification

XHEAL does not stop after identifying a problem. Its intervention system can generate countermeasure recommendations, explain why they were suggested and allow the crew to accept, adjust or decline them.

Interventions can include protected recovery periods, workload reduction, task redistribution and other configurable mission countermeasures.

After an intervention, the system observes subsequent measurements and evaluates whether the expected changes occurred. It distinguishes observed improvement from proven causation.

This creates a continuous process of detection, assessment, intervention, verification and reassessment.

What-If mission planning

I also developed a scenario engine that allows mission planners to examine possible changes before implementing them.

Scenarios can modify recovery time, workload, task schedules, environmental conditions, crew assignments or countermeasures.

The engine evaluates the resulting health, capability, schedule, crew and resource implications against an immutable baseline. It also accounts for uncertainty and compares trade-offs instead of automatically declaring one scenario the winner.

Psychological wellbeing

Psychological wellbeing is treated as a first-class part of the system rather than an optional feature.

XHEAL incorporates mood, stress, psychological recovery, social connection and behavioural changes. It distinguishes astronaut self-reports from inferred states and supporting physiological signals.

The system considers mission workload, isolation, schedule pressure and recovery conditions while maintaining privacy boundaries around personal psychological information.

NASA research integration

XHEAL integrates publicly available human spaceflight research from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.

Two datasets from the SpaceX Inspiration4 mission are currently imported:

  • OSD-575: Blood serum metabolic and immune/cardiac cytokine measurements, with 1,035 normalized observations.
  • OSD-569: Whole-blood and complete blood count measurements, with 553 normalized observations.

Together, these provide 1,588 normalized research observations from four human crew members across the available study timepoints.

The integration includes dataset discovery, downloading, parsing, scientific variable mapping, unit validation, subject and timepoint reconstruction, and source provenance.

These are discrete research observations, not continuous real-time astronaut telemetry. XHEAL preserves that distinction throughout the application.

Mission simulation and interface

To demonstrate the system as a complete mission workflow, I developed a deterministic synthetic Mars mission simulation covering SOL160–190, with two crew members and multiple physiological, environmental and operational signals.

The simulation includes changing workload, sleep restriction, elevated cabin CO2, cognitive degradation, sensor failure, recovery interventions and other mission events.

The frontend brings these systems together through Overview, Health, Mental, Capability, Live Data, Timeline, Interventions, What-If, Evidence, Copilot, Settings and NASA Research sections.

The Copilot acts as a conversational explanation layer over the system's structured outputs. It helps users understand assessments, evidence and mission scenarios without replacing the underlying deterministic reasoning.

Technology and engineering

The project uses Python for the scientific and mission-processing systems, FastAPI for backend services, and a modern web frontend built with the project's existing JavaScript/TypeScript framework and styling stack. Scientific processing uses tools including NumPy, pandas and SciPy. The application also integrates a generative AI provider for conversational assistance.

The system is organized into independently testable stages, with validation, reproducibility checks, data-quality controls and provenance tracking throughout.

Why I built it

I wanted to move beyond a dashboard that tells an astronaut what their measurements look like. I wanted to build something that connects those measurements to what the crew actually needs to accomplish.

For a long-duration mission, the important question is not just whether an astronaut's health has changed. It is what that change means for their work, what can be done about it, and whether the intervention made a difference.

XHEAL is a research and engineering prototype exploring that approach. It is not a certified medical device or an autonomous authority for flight-safety decisions. Its assessments and countermeasures require appropriate human oversight.
